article.title: Demonstrations throughout Colombia Target New President and US Intervention
article.author: MLToday
article.content: By W.T. Whitney Jr. October 21, 2026 The anti-government demonstrations that recently rocked Colombia erupted only two months after President Abelardo de la Espriella took office, on August 7. The framework surrounding them is large. Colombian academician Manuel Humberto Restrepo Domínguez refers to a “humanistic outburst against fascism and capitalism in its genocidal phase … circulating through the streets of major cities in Europe, Latin America, and — starting on October 14 — in Colombia.” On that day, Colombians pilloried both the new president and US pretensions. Demonstrations took place in 62 locations and the capital cities of all 31 departments. Marshalled against the far-right De la Espriella, a novice politician, were thousands of protesting and marching unionists, workers, students, teachers, feminists, indigenous people, past office holders, and veteran activists of all stripes. The outpouring of dissent was extraordinary. De la Espriella had succeeded Gustavo Petro, president of Colombia’s only progressive government, ever. Petro accompanied marchers in Bogota, as did Senator Iván Cepeda, the defeated presidential candidate of the Historic Pact Party, founded by Petro. The margin by which Cepeda lost was less than one percent. A US-facilitated social-media storm contributed to his defeat. On the day prior to October 14, De la Espriella fired up opposition forces by issuing his repressive Decree 1525. The measure stipulates that dialogue with protesters not “condition, suspend, or postpone enforcement actions directed individually against those who commit acts of violence.” In general, presidential decrees and slogans are setting the new government’s course, not legislation. Nelson Lombana Silva, blogger and Communist Party activist, characterizes the protests as a “national strike” and harbinger of an eventual general strike. Reporting from Ibagué, capital of Tolima Department, he condemns “the criminal ESMAD [riot control police] … [for] violently attacking artists and cultural activists, beating young people, children, and veteran [activists] …They had been chanting slogans against the nefarious government of death and despair. Tear gas flooded the park, spreading panic and state-sponsored terror.” Elsewhere, the police assaulted reporters and human rights defenders, arrested demonstrators, and employed tear gas, stun guns, and rubber bullets. In Medellín,tanks were used. A BBC report catalogues specific actions and interests of Colombia’s new government that are likely to be provoking opposition. A listing follows: • The government is preparing for cuts to the minimum wage and pensions. Concrete proposals are still lacking. • The government will no longer implement its 2016 Peace Agreement with former FARC leftist insurgents. Nor will it cooperate with the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, part of that agreement. • It prioritizes military action against armed groups and henceforth will not negotiate with the remaining leftist insurgencies and dissident FARC groups. • The government broke diplomatic relations with Nicaragua and Cuba and restored relations with Israel, whose influence in Colombia grows. • Colombia’s government is entering “a ‘cultural battle’ … [in favor of] traditional family values and Christian morality” • The new government joined the US-initiated Shield of the Americas, vehicle for US military intervention in the entire region • The report states that De la Espriella “does not dismiss [the idea] of Colombia withdrawing … from in the United Nations, the Organization of American States, and the Interamerican Court of Human Rights.” A recent flurry of “extrajudicial executions ” accompanying police and military actions outraged many Colombians. The BBC offers few details about Colombia’s tightened relationship with the U.S. government. Colombia’s new government has re-committed to joint US-Colombian war on drug traffickers. The US government, however, has long regarded its “drug war” as pretext for engaging leftist insurgents militarily and for providing support generally to Colombia’s military. As reported by the New York Times on October 14, 600 US troops will be heading soon to Colombia where they will carry out training exercises with the Colombian military. De la Espriella’s government has resurrected the failed approach of fumigating coca fields with carcinogenic glyphosate. His government’s military alignment with the US signals complicity with deadly US attacks on small coastal vessels supposedly carrying drugs. Colombia’s new government will likely grant free rein to US corporations, including extractive industries. The plundering that results would aggravate damage already visited upon Colombian land and the environment. Nelson Lombana Silva sounds the alarm: “In a short time, the illegal and mafia-like government of Abelardo de la Espriella has done so much harm … [I]n addition to surrendering national sovereignty, it has been giving away natural resources left and right, exposing the nation’s land to the risk of being turned into a vast desert … Oil and precious metals have fallen into the hands of imperialism thanks to the treacherous, sell-out policies of that clown of a president, Abelardo de la Espriella. He speaks Spanish but thinks in English.” This last remark is shorthand for identifying the president as a US citizen, longtime Miami resident, and wealthy lawyer. He made big money defending extradited Colombian narcotraffickers and top-level paramilitary chieftains in US courts. Lombana Silva resumes: “Counter-reform marches on with increased fracking, lay-offs of 700,000 workers, the highlands and water reservoirs being devastated, ecosystems destroyed, public education privatized, and dumbing down of students with religious indoctrination so they will no longer be thinking, critical individuals, but will remain submissive to Uncle Sam’s dictates .” Looking at the larger context, Professor Restrepo suggests that demonstrations in Colombia and Europe “represent the historical antagonism between capital … as led by government officials subordinate to the club of multi-billionaires allied with colonialist states, on one side, and on the other, the common people who … suffer exploitation, inequality, injustice, discrimination, exclusion, alienation and repression.” He adds that, “Out of that resistance arose the right to rebellion (to take up arms … and the right to social, civil, and unarmed protest.” Restrepo finds affirmation in, of all places, the United States, specifically in Henry David Thoreau’s Civil Disobedience (1849). He quotes: “All men recognize the right of revolution; that is, the right to refuse allegiance to, and to resist, the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable.” -W.T. Whitney Jr. is a retired pediatrician and political journalist living in Maine. The post Demonstrations throughout Colombia Target New President and US Intervention appeared first on MLToday .
